overview:
What became the largest European empire of the early modern world began not in the Americas but in the Atlantic islands off Africa. Castilian and Norman adventurers landed in the Canaries in 1402, and the slow, brutal subjugation of the indigenous Guanches over most of the next century — part private venture by nobles, part royal campaign under Ferdinand and Isabella — gave Spain both a template for conquest and a staging post for the Atlantic crossing. In 1492 Granada fell and Columbus sailed; two years later the Treaty of Tordesillas carved an imaginary line through an ocean neither signatory had crossed, assigning most of the Americas to Castile. Within a single generation Hernán Cortés had toppled the Aztec state (1519–21) and Francisco Pizarro the Inca (from 1532), though resistance persisted for decades and in the Maya lowlands until 1697. What made these conquests possible was less Spanish arms than Old World disease, indigenous allies with grievances of their own, and the political fractures inside the states being attacked.

The empire that followed was governed from Seville and Madrid through the Council of the Indies, the Casa de Contratación, and viceroyalties at Mexico City (1535) and Lima (1542), with local town councils and a dense apparatus of clergy underneath. Its engine was silver: Potosí in the Andes and Zacatecas and Guanajuato in Mexico, worked by coerced indigenous labour under rotational drafts and, increasingly on plantations and in cities, by enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic in Spanish-licensed trades. From Manila, taken in 1565, galleons ran Mexican silver to China and brought Asian goods back, closing the first genuinely global circuit of trade. American bullion also financed Habsburg wars in Europe, and after 1580 Spain briefly absorbed Portugal and its empire too. That wealth proved corrosive as much as sustaining — it fed inflation, chronic royal bankruptcy, and commitments Spain could not defend. The Bourbon reforms of the eighteenth century tried to tighten and tax the system; instead they helped alienate American-born elites. Between 1808 and 1833, with the monarchy shattered by Napoleon, almost all the mainland American territories broke away.

What remained shrank in stages. Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam were lost in the war with the United States in 1898, a defeat that convulsed Spanish politics and letters. Spain then held a scatter of African possessions — the Moroccan protectorate, relinquished in 1956, Equatorial Guinea, independent in 1968, and the Spanish Sahara. Under pressure from Moroccan claims and a Sahrawi insurgency, Spain withdrew from the Sahara in 1975 and formally ceded its administration in 1976, the date usually taken as the empire's end. The territory's status remains unresolved to this day, and Spain still holds Ceuta, Melilla and the Canaries.
significance: Few states have reshaped the planet so thoroughly or so unevenly. Spanish rule joined the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia into one exchange of crops, silver, microbes and people, seeding a demographic catastrophe in the Americas — indigenous populations fell by anywhere from three-quarters to over ninety per cent in the century after contact, on estimates that historians still dispute sharply — while making Spanish and Catholicism the language and faith of most of a hemisphere. Its silver monetised economies as far away as Ming China; its legal debates over whether indigenous peoples had rights, argued between figures like Las Casas and Sepúlveda, are a genuine root of modern international law; its racial and land-tenure hierarchies outlived it in the republics that replaced it. The map of Latin America, and much of the argument about colonialism itself, is downstream of this empire.
coverage: This was written from general reference works — Wikipedia's synthesis, an EBSCO research starter, and encyclopedia entries surfaced in search — rather than from specialist scholarship, and the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so the map can show nothing of its nearly six centuries. Two things are genuinely uncertain rather than merely thin here: the scale of the indigenous population collapse, where pre-contact estimates for the Americas range from under ten million to sixty million and the relative weight of disease, warfare, enslavement and social breakdown is actively contested; and the interior life of the conquered, which survives largely through documents written by Spanish officials and missionaries, with indigenous-authored sources such as the Nahuatl annals or Guaman Poma's chronicle rare and themselves shaped by colonial censorship.
